t01.P: CrossAMI is computed on the training window only because scores taken over the full series let test-window values leak into exogenous screening.
t01.N: CrossAMI for exogenous screening (F8) is computed on the training window only, and the leakage boundary is the train_end argument since version 0.3.
N_plus: Exogenous screening is step F8 in the rolling-origin evaluation guide.
The CrossAMI score for each driver is listed in the screening table.

t02.P: Passing a variable whose future values are not known at prediction time into known_future_drivers gives the model information it will not have in production.
t02.N: known_future_drivers takes a list of variable names, then stores the future values known at prediction time, such as calendar flags, in the forecasting config object.
N_plus: Calendar flags and planned promotions are the two examples given in the drivers guide.
The known_future_drivers argument was added to the forecasting config in release 0.4.

t03.P: If the informative horizon set comes back empty, no lag carries signal above the noise floor and model evaluation stops rather than targeting any horizon.
t03.N: Model evaluation targets the horizons in the informative horizon set of the result object, and the signal above the noise floor that each lag carries is kept as a float.
N_plus: Model evaluation in the tutorial uses the horizons listed in the informative horizon set.
The noise floor is drawn as a grey line in the horizon plot.

t04.P: A True is_non_monotone flag marks a profile with a later secondary peak, and the next action is to drop the monotone decay assumption and keep each lag.
t04.N: The is_non_monotone flag is a boolean field on the profile result, added in release 0.4 next to the monotone decay assumption column and the next_action field.
N_plus: Monotone decay is the shape most AMI profiles take in the worked examples.
The is_non_monotone flag sits next to the peak_lag field in the profile result.

t05.P: The engineering convention of dropping the normalization does not apply when the autocovariance feeds a significance test, which needs the Pearson correlation scale.
t05.N: The autocovariance normalized to a Pearson correlation coefficient is what the acf helper returns, and the engineering variant without normalization was added 3 months later.
N_plus: Time series analysis texts use the normalized form throughout their examples.
The engineering variant of the autocovariance is exposed as acovf in the stats module.

t06.P: A plot whose partial autocorrelations all fall inside the confidence interval after lag 3 gives an AR model order of 3, and the next step is to fit an AR(3) model.
t06.N: The partial autocorrelation plot is drawn by plot_pacf, then saved to the figures folder with the confidence interval shaded and each lag of the AR model order in the next panel.
N_plus: The AR model order section of the guide follows the autocorrelation section.
The confidence interval on the plot uses the Bartlett formula from the stats module.

t07.P: If a high score persists across multiple backends and sample-size stress testing, the warning is cleared; if it collapses, the inflation was numerical and the result is discarded.
t07.N: Numerical inflation is logged as a warning in the result object, since the multiple backends for sample-size stress testing are listed in the backends parameter of the run config file.
N_plus: The stress testing module lives under the diagnostics package.
Numerical inflation warnings carry the code NUM_INFLATION in the result object.

t08.P: The practice of attaching uncertainty does not hold for deterministic schedule values like fixed calendar holidays, which carry no forecast error at all.
t08.N: The interval_width column holds the uncertainty attached to each forecast under this practice, and the plotting helper draws it as a degree band around the line.
N_plus: Forecasts in the tutorial notebooks carry an interval_width column next to the point value.
The good practice note on uncertainty appears in the forecasting guide.

t09.P: Such lags are treated as leakage candidates because a derived feature built from the raw series cannot hold more information about the target than the raw profile.
t09.N: The derived-feature profile is computed first, then the raw profile, and each lag of both profiles is stored in the data-leakage candidate table with its estimation noise.
N_plus: The derived-feature profile uses the same AMI estimator as the raw profile.
The data-leakage candidate table is written to the reports folder.

t10.P: Surrogates give a series-specific noise floor, and without that floor a high AMI value at some lag cannot be told apart from chance dependence.
t10.N: Surrogates are drawn by the surrogate module, with sample size n and n_surrogates set at 200 and 99 by default since version 0.2 of the package.
N_plus: The surrogate module supports phase-randomised and block-shuffled surrogates.
The n_surrogates parameter is part of the diagnostics config.

t11.P: Epsilon is tied to the surrogate upper band so that the threshold scales with each series' own noise level instead of admitting noise lags in weak series.
t11.N: Epsilon is stored as a fraction of the surrogate upper band in epsilon_rel, and the global absolute threshold for noise lags in each series is named epsilon_abs.
N_plus: The surrogate upper band is computed per lag from the surrogate draws.
Epsilon appears in the horizon selection section of the guide.

t12.P: A symbol listed in public_api.md is part of the supported import contract and may be imported directly; any symbol absent from that list is internal and avoided.
t12.N: The public_api.md file lists each symbol that is part of the supported import contract and sits in the docs/reference folder, next to the changelog for release 0.4.
N_plus: Contributors edit public_api.md in the same pull request that adds a symbol.
The supported import contract covers the top-level package namespace.

t13.P: A new method label keeps earlier runs reproducible, since users who pinned cross_pami or xami_sparse would otherwise get different lags from the same call.
t13.N: New selectors such as PMIME-style or PC-stable are listed under the method label column, then documented next to the shipped cross_pami and xami_sparse in the table.
N_plus: The xami_sparse selector was shipped in release 0.5.
The method label for cross_pami is printed in every selection result.

t14.P: The practice does not hold for a point forecast fed straight into an automated order rule, where the downstream system accepts a single number and ignores any interval.
t14.N: The degree of uncertainty attaching to forecasts is stored as a 90% interval by default, in the interval column of the forecast frame returned by the point forecast call.
N_plus: Forecasts are returned as a frame with point and interval columns.
The good practice note on uncertainty cites the forecasting textbook.

t15.P: The terms are not interchangeable in engineering code when a function returns values bounded by one, since those are normalized autocorrelations.
t15.N: The normalization in engineering code is set by the normalize argument of the autocorrelation function, and autocovariance is its unnormalized output.
N_plus: Engineering texts use the term autocorrelation for the unnormalized sum.
The autocovariance function lives in the stats module.

t16.P: Train-window diagnostics in rolling-origin evaluation give fold scores that move gradually, and a sharp jump at one fold marks leakage that the next step traces.
t16.N: Rolling-origin evaluation stores the diagnostics computed on train windows in the fold_diagnostics table, one row per fold, keyed by origin date and window size.
N_plus: Train windows in rolling-origin evaluation grow by one step per fold.
The fold_diagnostics table is part of the evaluation result.

t17.P: The lower band stops being useless when a backend's bias pushes MI estimates below zero, since the lower band then shows how far the bias reaches.
t17.N: The upper band and the lower band for MI are returned as band_upper and band_lower, then drawn as dashed lines in the surrogate bands plot of the report.
N_plus: Surrogate bands are computed from the same draws for every lag.
The upper band appears in the profile plot as a dashed line.

t18.P: Backends whose lag ranks agree with linear_residual across the robustness study pipeline are kept, and a backend that reorders the top lags is dropped from the set.
t18.N: The robustness study pipeline writes its comparison of all configured backends against linear_residual to robustness.csv, then prints a summary table of the backends.
N_plus: The linear_residual backend is the reference estimator in the robustness study.
Configured backends are listed in the backends section of the config file.

t19.P: If new logic computes a diagnostic it belongs in the core package, and if it only formats or plots results it goes in the reporting layer described in architecture.md.
t19.N: The architecture.md file describes where new logic lives across the core package and the reporting layer, and it sits in the docs/explanation folder of the repository.
N_plus: Contributors open architecture.md from the contributing guide.
The core package and the reporting layer are separate subpackages for new logic.

t20.P: With 99 surrogates the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles fall on actual draws, and with fewer the band edges are interpolated guesses that misstate significance.
t20.N: The two-sided band uses 99 surrogates by default through the n_surrogates parameter, the significance threshold is the band_upper field, and fewer draws are refused.
N_plus: The surrogates for the band are drawn by the surrogate module.
The significance threshold appears as a dashed line in the profile plot.

t21.P: When fewer than two seasonal cycles of data are available, choose a seasonal naive method; with long histories and known drivers, choose a regression-based method.
t21.N: The forecasting method is selected through the method argument, and the objectives and available data are logged since release 0.3 in the run metadata file of each run.
N_plus: Selection of a forecasting method is covered in chapter three of the guide.
Available data are summarised in the run metadata before fitting.

t22.P: Horizons whose AMI sits above the surrogate band in the forecastability profile (F1) are chosen for modelling, and horizons below the band are left out.
t22.N: The forecastability profile (F1) is produced by run_profile(), then saved next to the AMI curves as profile.json, with horizons and bands stored per lag.
N_plus: AMI curves are computed by the ami module for every lag.
The forecastability profile (F1) is the first step of the workflow guide.

t23.P: F3 is run on such series because added lags that carry noise rather than signal make the curve keep rising, and that pattern is invisible in single-lag AMI.
t23.N: F3 is the cumulative lag curve in the diagnostics module, and its plot of longer lags against noise and signal for each series is saved in the f3_curve folder.
N_plus: The F3 curve is drawn next to the AMI profile in the report.
Longer lags are capped by the max_lag parameter of F3.

t24.P: Diagnostics computed on the full series use values from after the forecast origin, which makes every fold score look better than any live forecast could be.
t24.N: run_rolling_origin_evaluation() takes the forecast origin through its origin argument, and diagnostics computed manually take the same boundary as a cutoff index.
N_plus: The leakage boundary is described in the rolling-origin evaluation guide.
Diagnostics computed manually are written to the user's own output folder.
